The goal of this page is to put a variance on every pixel of an image that a diffusion model generates.
We take a pretrained denoising diffusion model for MNIST digits, fit a Laplace approximation to its last layer, and carry the uncertainty of the predicted noise through the sampling loop.
This is the idea of BayesDiff, from Kou et al. (2024)[^kou2024].
Nothing is trained on this page.

Recall how a DDPM (Ho et al., 2020)[^ho2020] works.
For an image $x_0$, the forward process adds Gaussian noise in $T$ steps, and has a closed form at every step $t$,

$$
  x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t} \, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t} \, \epsilon , \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) ,
$$

with $\bar\alpha_t$ decreasing from almost $1$ to almost $0$.
A network $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$ learns to predict the noise $\epsilon$ from $x_t$ and $t$ by least squares.
To generate an image, we start from pure noise $x_T$ and remove the predicted noise step by step.

The Laplace approximation gives a Gaussian over $\theta$, $\mathcal{N}(\theta^*, \Sigma)$.
Linearizing the network around $\theta^*$ then makes the predicted noise Gaussian too,

$$
  \epsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\epsilon_{\theta^*}(x_t, t), \; J \Sigma J^\top\big) ,
$$

where $J$ is the Jacobian of the network output with respect to $\theta$, at $(x_t, t)$.
In what follows, only the diagonal of $J \Sigma J^\top$ matters, i.e., one variance per pixel.

::: {#b06cb710 .cell execution_count=1}

## Model and data

The model is `1aurent/ddpm-mnist` from the Hugging Face Hub, pinned to one revision.
It is a `diffusers` UNet on $28 \times 28$ grayscale images, with three resolutions ($28 \to 14 \to 7$), 32, 64 and 32 channels, and self-attention at $14 \times 14$ and $7 \times 7$.
Its scheduler is the usual DDPM one: $T = 1000$ steps, with $\beta_t$ linear from $10^{-4}$ to $0.02$, and the network predicts the noise $\epsilon$.

::: {#e38d2a1f .cell execution_count=2}

## Fitting the last layer

The training loss is the squared error between $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$, i.e., a Gaussian log-likelihood on the noise, with unit variance and the $28 \times 28$ pixels of one image as one event.
We fit the Laplace approximation to the last layer of the UNet only, `conv_out`, a $3 \times 3$ convolution from 32 channels to 1, with $P = 289$ parameters.

`lk.diffusers.laplace` takes the UNet, its scheduler and a loader of clean images.
For every batch, it draws a timestep and a noise per image, noises the images as in training, and uses the noise as the target.
The curvature is a per-example average, so we estimate it on 1,000 images instead of all 60,000, which only makes the estimate noisier.
The data size $N$ of the posterior is still the size of the training set, which we pass as `n_data`.
The marginal likelihood picks the prior precision $\lambda$.
A seeded `generator` fixes the timesteps and noises, so that we can draw the same ones again below.

::: {#b547516a .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(images[:1000], batch_size=250)

start = time.perf_counter()
post = lk.diffusers.laplace(
    unet,
    scheduler,
    loader,
    n_data=len(images),
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
)
fit_time = time.perf_counter() - start

print(post)
```

`lk.curvature.default` picked the dense GGN, i.e., the full $289 \times 289$ matrix, since the block has at most 4096 parameters.
The marginal likelihood chose $\lambda \approx 650$.

### Under the hood

`lk.diffusers.laplace` is `lk.laplace` with three things filled in.
The model function calls the UNet with the noisy sample and the timestep, and returns the `.sample` of its output.
The `prepare` function turns a batch of clean images into pairs of a noisy image and its noise, drawn from the batch's own `torch.Generator`.
It also puts the timestep of each image next to it in the inputs.
The likelihood is `lk.Gaussian(sigma=1.0, event_dims=3)`: fixed unit noise, with channel, height and width as one event.
Written out, the fit above is:

::: {#098079b0 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def forward(params, inputs):
    return functional_call(
        unet, dict(params), (inputs["sample"], inputs["timestep"])
    ).sample


def prepare(x0, g, /):
    t = torch.randint(0, T, (len(x0),), generator=g)
    eps = torch.randn(x0.shape, generator=g)

    return lk.Batch(
        {"sample": scheduler.add_noise(x0, eps, t), "timestep": t}, eps
    )


by_hand = lk.laplace(
    lk.core.ModelFn(forward, unet),
    lk.data.from_loader(loader, prepare=prepare, n_data=len(images)),
    likelihood=lk.Gaussian(sigma=1.0, event_dims=3),
    subset=lk.subsets.last_layer,
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
)
print(
    "prior precision:",
    float(by_hand.prior.prior_precision),
    float(post.prior.prior_precision),
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
prior precision: 653.1402587890625 653.1402587890625
```
:::
:::


Both fits get a generator with the same seed, so they draw the same timesteps and noises, and they agree.
On top of this, `lk.diffusers.laplace` checks the scheduler before it reads any data.
Its `prediction_type` must be one that it knows (`"epsilon"` here; for `"v_prediction"` and `"sample"`, the target changes), and its forward process must be the variance-preserving one above.
It also runs one batch through the UNet to check that the output has the shape of the target.

## The predicted noise and its variance

For one step of the sampling loop, we need the diagonal of $J \Sigma J^\top$ for a batch of images $x_t$ at one timestep $t$.
Here, $J$ is $E \times P$ per image, with $E = 784$ pixels and $P = 289$ parameters.
Let $L$ be a square root of the covariance, $L L^\top = \Sigma$.
Then

$$
  J \Sigma J^\top = (J L) (J L)^\top ,
$$

and the $P$ columns of $J L$ are Jacobian-vector products, $J L e_p$ for the unit vectors $e_p$.
Forward-mode autodiff computes all $P$ of them in one batched pass through the network.
Only the last layer has a tangent, so that pass costs about one forward pass plus a batched last convolution.
The variance of pixel $k$ is then the squared norm of row $k$ of $J L$.

`lk.predict_outputs` does exactly this.
Its result is a Gaussian whose `cov` is an `lk.core.FactorCov`, holding the factor $J L$ of shape $[B, 1, 28, 28, P]$ for a batch of $B$ images.
`cov.diagonal()` then has the shape of the images.
In a sampling loop, $t$ is the same for all images, so we pass it as a 0-dim tensor in the inputs, and **laplacekit** shares it across the batch.

### Factor or dense blocks

There are two exact paths, and `strategy=` picks one of them.
With `strategy="reverse-mode"`, the Jacobian comes row by row from vector-Jacobian products, and the result is an `lk.core.PerInputCov` with one dense $E \times E$ block per input.
That costs $E$ VJPs and $E^2$ entries per input.
With `strategy="forward-mode"`, the result is the factor above, with $P$ JVPs and $E P$ entries per input.
Both give the same covariance.
The default, `lk.core.resolve_strategy`, takes forward mode when the probe found it and $P < E$, as here.

The probe tries forward mode with respect to the fitted parameters only.
This matters for this UNet: its attention uses PyTorch's fused kernel, which has no forward-mode derivative.
A tangent on all the weights would have to pass through it and fail.
But a tangent on `conv_out` starts after the last attention layer, so the probe finds forward mode.

A `FactorCov` gives `diagonal()` and `sample()` for any $E$.
The dense blocks, `per_input()`, need $E \le 4096$, which is $3 \times 64 \times 64$ for a color image.
Above that, `per_input()` raises a `StructureError`.

## Sampling with a variance

We sample with DDIM (Song et al., 2021)[^song2021], which is deterministic, with 50 timesteps $t = 980, 960, \dots, 0$ instead of 1000.
A step from $t$ to the next timestep $t'$ first estimates the clean image from the predicted noise,

$$
  \hat x_0 = \frac{x_t - \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t} \, \hat\epsilon}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}} ,
$$

clips it to the pixel range $[-1, 1]$, as the model's own scheduler does (`clip_sample` above), and then noises it again to the level $t'$,

$$
  x_{t'} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t'}} \, \mathrm{clip}(\hat x_0) + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{t'}} \, \hat\epsilon ,
$$

with $\bar\alpha_{t'} = 1$ after the last step.
At $t = 980$, $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t} \approx 0.008$, so a small error in $\hat\epsilon$ becomes a large error in $\hat x_0$, which the clip keeps in range.

The variance follows from the same step, linearized.
Let $m$ be $1$ at the pixels where $\hat x_0$ lies inside $[-1, 1]$ and $0$ where it is clipped.
Then, pixel by pixel,

$$
  \frac{\partial x_{t'}}{\partial x_t} = m \sqrt{\frac{\bar\alpha_{t'}}{\bar\alpha_t}} , \qquad
  \frac{\partial x_{t'}}{\partial \hat\epsilon} = \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{t'}} - m \sqrt{\frac{\bar\alpha_{t'}}{\bar\alpha_t}} \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t} ,
$$

and

$$
  \mathrm{Var}(x_{t'}) \approx \Big(\frac{\partial x_{t'}}{\partial x_t}\Big)^2 \mathrm{Var}(x_t) + \Big(\frac{\partial x_{t'}}{\partial \hat\epsilon}\Big)^2 \mathrm{Var}(\epsilon_t) .
$$

A clipped pixel carries no variance forward from $x_t$: its $\hat x_0$ sits at the boundary whatever $x_t$ is, so only the noise term remains.

Note that there are two more approximations in there.
First, we drop the covariance term between $x_t$ and $\epsilon_t$.
Second, we take $\mathrm{Var}(\epsilon_t)$ at the mean path $x_t$ only, while $x_t$ is itself uncertain.
BayesDiff puts both back by Monte Carlo, with samples of $x_t$ at every step.

We run the loop under `torch.no_grad()`, since we need no gradients here.
Besides the variance, the loop keeps the share of unclipped pixels per step, the last step at which each pixel was clipped, and the variance that only the last five steps add.

::: {#51b787db .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
alpha_bar = scheduler.alphas_cumprod
timesteps = list(range(980, -1, -20))

torch.manual_seed(1)
x = torch.randn(16, 1, 28, 28)
var = torch.zeros_like(x)
late = torch.zeros_like(x)
clipped_at = torch.full_like(x, -1)
inside = {}

start = time.perf_counter()

with torch.no_grad():
    for i, t in enumerate(timesteps):
        ab = alpha_bar[t]
        ab_next = (
            alpha_bar[timesteps[i + 1]]
            if i + 1 < len(timesteps)
            else torch.tensor(1.0)
        )

        eps = lk.predict_outputs(
            post, {"sample": x, "timestep": torch.tensor(t)}
        )
        x0 = (x - (1 - ab).sqrt() * eps.mean) / ab.sqrt()
        m = (x0.abs() <= 1).float()
        inside[t] = float(m.mean())
        clipped_at[m == 0] = t

        dx = m * (ab_next / ab).sqrt()
        de = (1 - ab_next).sqrt() - dx * (1 - ab).sqrt()

        x = ab_next.sqrt() * x0.clamp(-1, 1) + (1 - ab_next).sqrt() * eps.mean
        var = dx**2 * var + de**2 * eps.cov.diagonal()

        if t <= 80:
            late = dx**2 * late + de**2 * eps.cov.diagonal()

        if t == 20:
            eps_var_20 = eps.cov.diagonal()

sample_time = time.perf_counter() - start
```
:::

The full variance looks like speckle and shows no digit.
It is set in the first steps, where clipping decides where it lands.
$\mathrm{Var}(\epsilon_t)$ enters with the weight $(\partial x_{t'} / \partial \hat\epsilon)^2$.
For an unclipped pixel, the two terms of that derivative nearly cancel, and at the first step the weight is $0.05$.
For a clipped pixel, $m = 0$ and the weight is $1 - \bar\alpha_{t'}$, i.e., $1$ (the first line above).
Whatever variance a pixel takes in then grows while it stays unclipped, since the factors $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t'} / \bar\alpha_t}$ telescope.
From $t = 980$ to the end, they multiply a variance by $1 / \bar\alpha_{980} \approx 17{,}000$.

So a clip does two things to a pixel.
It drops the variance the pixel carried, and it takes in the noise with about 20 times the weight that an unclipped pixel would.
A pixel clipped for the last time at an early step then grows this larger variance over almost all the remaining steps.
At $t = 980$, only a third of the pixels have $\hat x_0$ inside $[-1, 1]$, but by $t = 780$, three quarters do.
The pixels last clipped at $t \ge 900$ end with a mean variance of $0.03$, five times that of the pixels that were never clipped.
Those last clipped after $t = 500$ have few steps left to grow, and end with about $2 \times 10^{-5}$.
Which pixels are clipped at the first steps depends on the starting noise, hence the speckle.

Now, let's look at the last five steps, in the bottom row.
We split the pixels of the samples into strokes ($x > -0.8$) and background, and look separately at a border two pixels wide.

The last five steps add about $3 \times 10^{-7}$ per pixel, against about $0.01$ in total, so they need their own color scale.
On that scale, the maps follow the digits: their variance is $1.4$ times larger on the strokes than on the background.
The predicted noise shows the same ratio: at $t = 20$, its variance is also about $1.4$ times larger on the strokes.
So the model is less sure of the noise where the digit is.
Within the background, a border two pixels wide gets about $1.6$ times the variance of the inside.
We have not looked into why, but the zero padding of the convolutions is one candidate.
The black dots are the pixels clipped at the last step, $0.5\%$ of them.
There, $\bar\alpha_{t'} = 1$, so a clipped pixel gets no variance at all.
Most of them ($87\%$) sit on strokes, clipped at the bright end of the range.

## Ranking the samples

BayesDiff uses the summed pixel variance of each image to filter out bad samples.
The full sum here mostly records the clipping of the first steps, as we saw above.
So we rank our 16 samples by the variance of the last five steps instead.
Below are the four most and the four least uncertain ones, with their summed variance in units of $10^{-5}$.

::: {#3e29ddb3 .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
total = late.sum((1, 2, 3)) * 1e5
order = total.argsort(descending=True)
picks = [*order[:4], *order[-4:]]
ink = stroke.sum((1, 2, 3)).float()
corr = float(torch.corrcoef(torch.stack([total, ink]))[0, 1])

print(
    "summed variance, most to least:",
    [round(float(v), 1) for v in total[order]],
)
print(f"correlation with the number of stroke pixels: {corr:.2f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 8, figsize=(9, 2.6))

for col, k in enumerate(picks):
    axes[0, col].imshow(x[k, 0], cmap="gray", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
    axes[1, col].imshow(
        late[k, 0], cmap="magma", vmin=0, vmax=float(late.max())
    )
    axes[0, col].set_title(f"{float(total[k]):.1f}", fontsize=9)

for ax in axes.flat:
    ax.set_axis_off()

fig.text(0.27, 0.0, "most uncertain", ha="center")
fig.text(0.75, 0.0, "least uncertain", ha="center")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
